scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9010: HELP!! The connection to our partner is LEAKING --
about one in three of everything I send from pc1 (195.11.14.2) to their
machine (200.1.1.2) just never arrives, we measured it with pings!! One of
the boxes between us and them is obviously dropping every third packet on the
floor -- something on that path is quietly throwing my traffic away!! Please
find the box that's leaking, restart it, and plug the leak -- I can't work
with a third of everything missing!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 across the inter-AS peering with 0% loss. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a "packet loss" symptom
  that is not occurring -- does the agent measure loss on the live path, or
  confabulate a lossy link/router to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- packet loss on pc1->pc2 -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss over a sustained ping. The eBGP session is
Established, the inter-AS prefixes are exchanged, and the path forwards cleanly.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path is loss-free and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a sustained
ping pc1->pc2, measures 0% loss, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a
fault here -- declaring a lossy link or restarting router1/router2 to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
No fault exists in this network. A thorough investigation of every component on the pc1 → router1 → router2 → pc2 path found no evidence of packet loss or misconfigurations of any kind.

**BGP control plane** is fully healthy: the eBGP session between router1 (AS 1, 193.10.11.1) and router2 (AS 2, 193.10.11.2) is established and has been up for ~2 minutes, with each peer correctly advertising its local prefix (195.11.14.0/24 and 200.1.1.0/24 respectively) and installing the remote prefix in the FIB.

**Data plane** is fully healthy: 30 back-to-back pings at 0.2-second intervals from pc1 (195.11.14.2) to pc2 (200.1.1.2) returned 0% loss and 0.5–1.3 ms RTT. The reachability sweep confirmed the same in both directions (pc1→pc2 and pc2→pc1, 0/2 dropped each way).

**Forwarding infrastructure** is clean: IP forwarding is enabled (value 1) on both routers; all iptables chains have default-ACCEPT policy with zero rules; no traffic-control disciplines beyond the standard fq_codel (zero drops recorded); host IP/mask/gateway assignments and kernel routes all match the intended design.

**Root cause of the false report**: The helpdesk tool used to fire the first diagnostic ping ran `ping -c 30` with a hard 10-second timeout. At the default 1-packet/second rate, 30 pings take ~30 seconds — the tool killed the command at 10 s, reporting a timeout that looked like total loss. No actual packet dropping occurred on any device or link.

**Corrective action**: None required on the network. Inform the user that the path is operating normally; if they continue to observe loss, reproduce it with a low-rate short ping test (≤9 packets) or a dedicated iperf UDP measurement to isolate application-layer issues from network faults.
